etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Latin diagnōsis, from Ancient Greek διάγνωσις (diágnōsis), from διαγιγνώσκω (diagignṓskō, “to discern”), from διά (diá, “through”) + γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “to know”).

definitions.definition: (medicine, countable, uncountable) The process of, or an instance of, identification of the nature and cause of an illness.

quote.citation: 2012 January, Philip E. Mirowski, “Harms to Health from the Pursuit of Profits”, in American Scientist‎[1], volume 100, number 1, archived from the original on 4 April 2012, page 87:
quote.text: In an era when political leaders promise deliverance from decline through America’s purported preeminence in scientific research, the news that science is in deep trouble in the United States has been as unwelcome as a diagnosis of leukemia following the loss of health insurance.

definitions.definition: The process of, or an instance of, identification of the nature and cause of something (of any nature).

quote.citation: 1887, Charles L. Reade, Compton Reade, Charles Reade, Dramatist, Novelist, Journalist: A Memoir:
quote.text: The quick eye for effects, the clear diagnosis of men's minds, and the love of epigram.
My diagnosis of his character proved correct.

definitions.definition: (taxonomy) A written description of a species or other taxon serving to distinguish that species from all others; especially a description written and published in Latin.

quote.citation: 1992, Rudolf M[athias] Schuster, The Hepaticae and Anthocerotae of North America: East of the Hundredth Meridian, volume V, Chicago, Ill.: Field Museum of Natural History, →ISBN, page viii:
quote.text: The repeated exposure, over decades, to most taxa here treated has resulted in repeated modifications of both diagnoses and discussions, as initial ideas of the various taxa underwent—often repeated—conceptual modification.

quote.citation: 2013, Donald A. Norman, The Design of Everyday Things:
quote.text: Experienced mechanics can diagnosis the condition of machinery just by listening.
